rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but a monitoring organisation documents that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace; a local group provides safe housing for LGBT youth fleeing family violence. No legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law; the community organises underground.
rewrites.blindTangential: Anti-gay lynching pattern — trans people are among the most visible targets of perceived-LGBT violence; same-sex conduct itself is legal.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: No legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination law — resident-facing gaps; the local group's safe housing serves local youth.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Lynching pattern is documented climate, not statute.
blindSourceSummaries: A monitoring organisation (9 Apr 2024): a local safe-housing club has housed LGBT+ youth since about 2020 — a temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from the country and the sub-region have passed; the framing is that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace. Current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

An organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised anywhere in the country, but sexual-orientation-and-gender discrimination is not prohibited, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

A government annual human-rights report: the law does not explicitly prohibit sexual-orientation-and-gender discrimination; LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised; the community — especially outside major urban areas — faces hostility, with LGBTQI+ persons routinely refused medical care (including hormone treatment) and social services. Official assessment of on-the-ground hostility and service denial, with an urban/rural split visitors should weigh.

A news outlet (31 Aug 2015): LGBT people in several countries of the region describe discrimination and persecution from both churches and their governments. Regional religious-institution hostility relevant to this country — dated 2015, treat as context not current-evidence.

A monitoring organisation (8 May 2012): an interview with a researcher citing evidence of same-sex relationships in this country alongside several regional countries, and an anthropologist's record of women-women marriages in ancient times in the same country; frames same-sex practice as indigenous rather than a historic-era import. Historical baseline supporting the framing that today's statutory legality sits on long-standing practice, not recent liberalisation.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors — and newly criminalising: in March 2025 the governing military authority's founding charter explicitly outlawed “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the first time. Military rule, an insurgency, no recourse.
rewrites.blindTangential: The March 2025 charter explicitly criminalises “LGBTQIA+ practices” — trans visitors are named targets of the new provision.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: March 2025 criminalisation is brand new; enforcement undocumented.
blindSourceSummaries: An organisation's country overview (updated 12 March 2026): in March 2025 the country explicitly outlawed same-sex acts for the first time — a provision of the governing military authority's founding charter bans 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition following the 2023 coup. No specific penalties are set yet, but a 2023 draft penal code proposes up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/officiating/witnessing a same-sex marriage and five years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Earlier in 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under a public-indecency provision (up to three years) and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them; the code fixes age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts versus 13 for different-sex acts.

A news outlet live page (December 2022): the country's lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships — weeks after a court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships. Documents the legislative trail into the 2025 criminalisation.

A news outlet (1 July 2026): at least 40 people have been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men — including high-ranking military officials — imprisoned across the country following the introduction of a new penal code earlier in 2026, in what campaigners describe as a 'witch-hunt' with a 'toxic' climate; sources also fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence as access to preventive medication collapses. Current enforcement evidence for the record.

An official news agency (in the national language): headline 'the country criminalises LGBTQIA+ practice' — official press announcement of the criminalisation. Page body was largely navigation content at fetch time; headline finding only.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2017 (misdemeanour, up to 2 years); military-adjacent governance; no legal gender recognition; no community infrastructure; very thin data.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2017 (up to 2 years) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
blindSourceSummaries: A government annual human-rights report: the criminalisation section states the law criminalised consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults with punishments ranging from three months to two years' imprisonment — official current-law baseline for visitor exposure; the report also covers societal abuses.

A government 2010 human-rights report (pre-criminalisation baseline): the law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts' with no evidence it was used against LGBT persons that year; no known LGBT organisations and few reports of violence, most persons discreet due to social strictures — documents the pre-2017 legal climate.
A government 2006 human-rights report: documents the then-regime's abuses — extrajudicial killings, torture, peacekeeping withdrawal — general context.

A news analysis: while further criminalisation attempts failed in some regional countries, they succeeded in this one and another — situates the country's criminalisation drive within the broader wave of conservative anti-LGBT advocacy, relevant context for how the law's trajectory developed.
rewrites.notes: substitution-only blind derivation per LANE_SPECS rule 7/7e: proper names, regime name, acronyms genericised; no new descriptors.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country demands real caution — and on a surprising positive trajectory: after briefly criminalising same-sex intimacy in 2019, it decriminalised in 2020, and in November 2024 voters ratified a new constitution that rejected calls to criminalise homosexuality. No legal gender recognition; social conservatism; but the constitutional debate is now public and the pro-criminalisation side lost.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2020 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 constitution rejected criminalisation.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: 2020 decriminalisation + 2024 constitution are formal; social climate lags.
blindSourceSummaries: An organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): criminalised same-sex intimacy in 2019 (max 6 months plus a fine), repealed in 2020 after upper-house approval — a reversal that sharply divided public opinion; the Nov-2024 constitution (under military government since Aug-2023) codifies privacy but retains a marriage definition; no legal gender recognition, LGBTI groups cannot register; same-sex relations legal for men and women.

A monitoring organisation (25 Nov 2024): the country's new constitution was ratified by referendum 16 Nov 2024 (over 90% yes, ~55% turnout) and rejected civil-society demands to re-criminalise homosexuality, adding LGBT+-protective privacy provisions — but codifies a marriage definition excluding same-sex couples. Context: the Aug-2023 military coup ended decades of long-ruling family governance.
A government 2019 human-rights report: official assessment covering the year the new penal code criminalised same-sex conduct — documents the legal change and societal discrimination.

A news outlet (13 Dec 2019): the country criminalised same-sex relations by law passed quietly in July 2019 — up to 6 months plus a fine; two men already arrested and released only after paying police bribes; the country inherited no historic-era sodomy law (independence in 1960). Enforcement precedent: arrests occurred within months of enactment — later reversed by the 2020 repeal.
A news outlet (July 2020): the country formally decriminalised homosexuality — the national legislature overturned the 2019 ban, restoring the pre-2019 status where same-sex conduct was not criminal.

A local news outlet (29 Oct 2019, in the national language): a 2019 law (new penal code) criminalises same-sex relations without naming 'homosexuality' — a provision files same-sex relations under attacks on morals; earlier in 2013 police arrested and later released two alleged offenders. Primary-source detail on the criminalisation year (2019) later reversed in 2020.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Same-sex conduct has been criminalised since 2009 (2 years), and the president himself has called for mob violence: in December 2023, the president said LGBT people should be “taken to a stadium and stoned” because “that's what they deserve” — condemned by a human-rights organisation as stoking fear; a local rights group called it a call to lynching. There is no legal gender recognition, no community infrastructure (the oldest rights group works from exile), and arbitrary detention is routine.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised since 2009 — the vehicle by which trans people (legally their birth sex) are prosecuted; also a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Presidential incitement is documented by a human-rights organisation (Jan 2024).
blindSourceSummaries: A human-rights organisation (Jan 2024): a report on the president stoking fear among LGBT people — the president's call to 'stone' homosexuals; the organisation urges the ruling party to renounce persecution.

A news outlet (Jan 2024): after the president called for 'homosexuals to be stoned', LGBTQ people reported terror; a rights league in exile called the remarks 'a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people'. Members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described the remarks as 'a real license to kill (us)'. Same-sex relations are criminalised in this country.

A government 2015 human-rights report: documents the country's crisis (extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention, media shutdowns) and includes the section on acts of violence and discrimination against LGBT persons — same-sex conduct criminalised since 2009, with arrests and harassment documented.
A government 2009 human-rights report (archived): covers the year the penal code criminalised same-sex conduct; documents discrimination against gays and lesbians.
A government 2010 human-rights report: lists discrimination against gays and lesbians among common human-rights abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture and harsh prison conditions.
A government 2012 human-rights report: documents torture, extrajudicial executions, prolonged pretrial detention, and discrimination against LGBT persons under the criminalised framework.

rewrites.blindSummary: This country is dangerous for trans visitors. The penal code criminalises same-sex conduct (3 years); a 2024 review stakeholder report documents violence and discrimination from both government and non-government actors; military rule since 2021; no legal gender recognition.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalised (3 years) — trans visitors captured via birth-sex status and partner risk.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Military rule; documented government and non-government violence.
blindSourceSummaries: A human-rights organisation's review stakeholder report on the country (Oct 2024): the country criminalises consensual same-sex relations while police commit arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion that deepen stigma and fear; LGBTQ+ people live in a hostile, sometimes lethal environment with threats of physical violence and discrimination on orientation, gender-identity and expression grounds.

A government 2023 human-rights report: official assessment — same-sex conduct criminalised under indecency provisions; documents violence and discrimination against LGBT persons and police harassment.

A human-rights organisation's joint review stakeholder report (Oct 2024) on LGBT+ rights: criminalisation of consensual same-sex activity; police arbitrary arrests, harassment and extortion; a hostile and 'sometimes deadly' environment; widespread stigmatisation hinders reporting of violence.
A government 2011 human-rights report: documents security-force torture, prison abuse, harmful traditional practice, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

A reference encyclopaedia entry on LGBT rights in the country (current): a provision of the 2016 penal code punishes same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine, or both; enforcement operates through arrests based on clothing and appearance, releases commonly bought by payment to police, and the law used as a basis for extortion; no legal gender recognition.
